 3   Q.     PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 4   A.     My name is Andrew K. Harriger. My business address is 100 E. Main Cross Street, Suite

 6

 7   Q.     WHAT IS YOUR PRESENT OCCUPATION?

 8   A.     I am a consultant at Sawvel and Associates, Inc. (“Sawvel”). Sawvel, a professional

 9          consulting firm founded in 1951, provides a wide range of services including cost of service

10          and rate studies, economic planning studies, power supply and generation planning,

11          financial planning and analysis, expert testimony, and contract negotiations.

12

13   Q.     WHAT IS YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND?

14   A.     I graduated from the University of Toledo with a Bachelor of Science Degree in Electrical

15          Engineering Technology. I am a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics

16          Engineers and the American Public Power Association.

17

19   A.     I have been employed at Sawvel for nineteen years. I have experience in the areas of public

20          utility planning, financing, and operations for electric and natural gas utility systems. My

21          professional experience includes class cost of service studies, rate design, planning and

22          analytical studies, feasibility studies and economic analyses. I have conducted detailed

 5          REGULATORY BODIES?

 6   A.     Yes, I have presented testimony before the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the

 7          New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (“NMPRC” or “Commission”). I have also

 3   Q.     WHAT WERE YOU ASKED BY THE COUNTY TO ADDRESS IN THIS

 4          PROCEEDING?

 7          1.   EPE’s cost allocation, revenue allocation and rate design for Rate 7.

 8          2.   EPE’s alternative class cost of service analysis with all City/County accounts served

 9               by Rate 7.

10          3.   Large Load Tariff Schedules.

12   Q.     PLEASE EXPLAIN THE APPROACH TO YOUR ANALYSIS?

13   A.     I began by reviewing EPE’s 2026 Application for Revision of Retail Electric Rates

14          Pursuant to Advice Notice No. 317. I then reviewed EPE’s class cost of service analysis

15          with particular attention to Rate 7. I reviewed EPE’s proposed allocation methods and its

16          reasoning behind those methods. I also reviewed EPE’s proposed revenue allocation and

17          rate design. During this review I assessed the appropriateness of EPE’s class cost of service

18          allocation methods, rate class revenue allocation and rate design for Rate 7.

19

20          I reviewed EPE’s proposed Large Load Tariffs (Rate 50 and Rate 51) and the proposed

21          Energy Service Agreement for large loads that would be served by Rate 50 and Rate 51.

22          I was not asked to review EPE’s jurisdictional cost of service analysis. I focused on the

23          New Mexico class cost of service analysis. The County has retained Mark Garrett to

 2          David Garrett to address depreciation and cost of capital.

 3

 4          I also reviewed the Company’s Amended Filing version of all documents previously

 5          described. All references in my testimony to EPE testimony, exhibits and workpapers

 6          should be assumed to be the Amended Filing version of the documents unless otherwise

 7          noted.

 9   Q.     PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR FINDINGS.

10   A.     My findings are as follows:

11                   1. EPE’s cost allocation and rate design methodologies for Rate 7 are appropriate.

12                   2. EPE’s Alternative CCOS with all City/County customers served by Rate 7 is

13                      insufficient and not supported by a functional CCOS model and workpapers.

14                   3. EPE should be required to provide fully functional cost of service model and

15                      workpapers for the Rate 7 Alternative CCOS and provide detailed explanation

16                      of the billing unit discrepancy so the County can properly evaluate opening Rate

17                      7 to new and existing customers.

18                   4. EPE’s proposed phase-in of base revenue requirement increases is not

19                      appropriate.

20                   5. Allocated revenue increases should be applied to each rate class using a banding

21                      approach with a 21% cap, 13.94% floor and phased in over a minimum of two

22                      years with a maximum 10% annual increase to limit rate shock for customers.

 1   Q.     HOW DO YOU RECOMMEND MODERATING RATE INCREASES OF THIS

 3   A.     I recommend using a banding revenue allocation method to determine the total revenue

 4          adjustments for each class. I would also recommend using no less than 12 months of gap

 7   Q.     WHAT IS A BANDING APPROACH TO REVENUE ALLOCATION?

 8   A.     A banding approach limits rate changes using a “band” around the system average increase.

 9          For example, if the band is set at +/- 25%, a 10% system increase would have an upper

10          band 12.5% and a lower band of 7.5%. In this scenario, each rate class would be limited

11          to a maximum rate change of 12.5% and a minimum rate change of 7.5%.

18   Q.     WHAT IS A DEMAND RATCHET?

19   A.     A demand ratchet is a rate design mechanism used to ensure a minimum amount of demand

20          revenue is collected even if customer loads vary significantly. An electric utility needs

21          sufficient transmission, distribution and generation capacity to serve customer loads during

22          all months of the year. Using a demand ratchet helps prevent a portion of those costs

23          shifting from customers with varying monthly demands to customers with steady monthly


     Sawvel and Associates, Inc.                  15
                                       DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                      ANDREW K. HARRIGER
                                    NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT

 1          demands. A demand ratchet is typically a percent of the maximum demand in the prior 12

 2          months or in the case of EPE the maximum demand during June through September using

 3          a historical rolling 12-month period.

 4

 5   Q.     WHAT ARE THE DEMAND RATCHETS FOR RATE 3, RATE 4 AND RATE 7?

 6   A.     The demand ratchet for Rate 3 is 60% of the maximum demand established during the

 7          billing months of June through September in the preceding twelve (12) month period. The

 8          demand ratchet for Rate 4 and Rate 7 is 65% for the same months.

 9

10   Q.     WHAT IS A MINIMUM DEMAND?

11   A.     While a demand ratchet moves with customer demand, a minimum demand for a rate class

12          is a fixed kW amount. It is typically set at the minimum qualifying demand for the rate

13          class.

14

15   Q.     WHAT ARE THE MINIMUM DEMANDS FOR RATE 3, RATE 4 AND RATE 7?

16   A.     The minimum demand for Rate 3 is 15 kW. The minimum demand for Rate 4 is 50 kW.

17          Rate 7 does not have a fixed minimum demand.
